Fact (IRS Pub 334 (2025), Cost of Goods Sold + Schedule C lines 35-42): cost of goods sold = beginning inventory + purchases and other costs - inventory at end of year; the closing inventory is subtracted and the remainder is cost of goods sold. ig_caption:
Myth: every dollar of stock you bought in 2026 is a 2026 write-off.
Fact: you deduct the cost of the goods you sold. What's still on the shelf on Dec 31 waits.

✔️ Cost of goods sold = stock at the start of the year + what you bought - stock left at year end.
✔️ Example: $0 at the start, $30,000 bought, $8,000 left on Dec 31. Your 2026 cost of goods sold is $22,000, not $30,000.
✔️ Smaller sellers can use simpler methods, but unsold stock still waits until it sells.

Count what's left on Dec 31 (warehouse, garage and Amazon FBA) and write the number down.

li_caption:
Many online sellers expect every dollar of stock bought this year to reduce this year's taxable profit. The IRS cost of goods sold rules work differently.

You deduct the cost of what you sold. Stock still on hand on December 31 is subtracted and carries into next year.

1. Start with inventory at the beginning of the year.
2. Add purchases and other product costs.
3. Subtract inventory at the end of the year. The remainder is cost of goods sold.

Example: a seller starts 2026 with no stock, buys $30,000 of products and has $8,000 left on December 31. Cost of goods sold for 2026 is $22,000, not $30,000. The $8,000 is deducted when those items sell.

Smaller businesses can choose simpler inventory methods, but unsold stock generally still waits until it is sold.

Before December 31, plan a count of everything on hand: home, storage unit and marketplace warehouses such as Amazon FBA. Write down the quantity and cost.

sources.fact: Cost of goods sold: beginning inventory plus purchases and other costs, minus inventory at end of year (Schedule C line 41 subtracted from line 40 gives line 42); the remainder is cost of goods sold during the tax year (IRS Pub 334 (2025), Cost of Goods Sold, read 2026-11-19)

Small business taxpayers (average annual gross receipts at or under the indexed threshold for the 3 prior years) may choose not to keep an inventory and instead treat inventory as non-incidental materials and supplies or follow their books (IRS Pub 334 (2025), read 2026-11-19)
$30,000 / $8,000 / $22,000 example is an illustration of the formula, not a client or statistic
